questions.question: Why do similar matrices $A$ and $P^{-1}AP$ have the same trace?
options: because $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$
because they have the same size
because trace ignores signs
because $P$ is invertible

questions.question: Is $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(A)\,\operatorname{tr}(B)$ in general?
options: Yes, for diagonal matrices
No, it generally fails
Yes, for all square matrices
Yes, whenever $A,B$ commute

questions.question: Why is trace defined here for square matrices?
options: Rectangular matrices have no entries at all.
It sums entries $a_{ii}$ along a full main diagonal.
Trace is the same as matrix multiplication.
Only square matrices have rows.

questions.question: How is trace different from determinant?
options: Trace and determinant are always equal.
Trace multiplies diagonal entries in every matrix.
Trace sums diagonal entries; determinant is multiplicative
Determinant is defined only for diagonal matrices.

questions.question: What eigenvalue fact is linked to trace?
options: The product of eigenvalues equals the trace.
The eigenvalue sum, with algebraic multiplicity, equals the trace
Every eigenvalue is equal to the trace.
Trace is defined only when all eigenvalues are real.

questions.question: What is $\operatorname{tr}\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$?
What is $\operatorname{tr}(I_4)$?
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&5&0\\1&-3&4\\7&8&6\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\operatorname{tr}(A)$?
If a $3\times3$ matrix has diagonal entries $a$, $b$, and $c$, what is its trace?
options: $a-b+c$
$abc$
$a+b+c$

questions.question: What is the trace of $\operatorname{diag}(4,-1,2)$?
For matrices with both $AB$ and $BA$ defined, which always holds even when $AB\neq BA$?
options: $\det(AB)=0$
$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=0$
$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$
$AB=BA$

questions.question: If two matrices have the same diagonal but different off-diagonal entries, what happens to their traces?
options: Their traces are equal.
They cannot have eigenvalues.
Their determinants must be equal.
Their traces must be different.

questions.question: How are trace and determinant linked to eigenvalues?
options: Trace is the product of eigenvalues; determinant is their sum.
Trace is the sum of eigenvalues; determinant is their product.
Neither is related to eigenvalues.
Both are the largest eigenvalue.

questions.question: A $2\times2$ matrix has eigenvalues $3$ and $-1$. What is its trace?
A $3\times3$ matrix has trace $7$ and two diagonal entries $2$ and $-1$. What is the third diagonal entry?
If $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&100\\-50&2\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\operatorname{tr}(A)$?
Why must algebraic multiplicity be mentioned in the eigenvalue sum statement?
options: Trace is undefined when an eigenvalue repeats.
Multiplicity changes the diagonal entries directly.
Repeated eigenvalues must be counted the correct number of times.
Only distinct eigenvalues are ever counted.

questions.question: Why should trace not be used as a test for invertibility?
options: Trace zero may be invertible; nonzero trace may be singular
Invertibility is determined only by off-diagonal entries.
Trace is not defined for square matrices.
A nonzero trace always means determinant zero.

questions.question: A $2\times2$ matrix has trace $0$ and determinant $-4$. If one eigenvalue is $2$, what is the other?
Give the trace of $A+B$ if $\operatorname{tr}(A)=3$ and $\operatorname{tr}(B)=-5$.
